title: SYSK Selects: How Crime Scene Cleanup Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2010 episode "How Crime Scene Cleanup Works." Chuck introduces it as a pick from September 7, 2010. The hosts cover the crime and trauma scene decontamination (CTSD) industry: how it differs from movie portrayals like Curdled and Sunshine Cleaning, the physical and emotional demands of the job, the three main scene types (violent death, decomposition, meth labs), tools and equipment, disposal and incineration rules, training and gross-out testing, turnover and stress disorders, business costs and marketing, and the ethics of profiting from tragedy. The episode closes with listener mail from a former federal prison inmate about commissary trade, escapes, and prison slang.

entities.name: Neil Smithers Crime Scene Cleaners, Inc.

segments.title: Rerun intro and movie banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Selects episode, originally from September 7, 2010. Josh and Chuck discuss the movies Curdled and Sunshine Cleaning and how far off their portrayals of cleanup work are.

segments.title: What CTSD cleanup is and why it is decontamination
segments.summary: CTSD (crime and trauma scene decontamination) is described as a niche, heavy-duty cleaning service requiring full biohazard suits. Cleanup goes beyond cleaning to restoring the scene to its original condition, which can mean cutting out carpet and baseboards.

segments.title: Who does this work and the personal demands
segments.summary: Workers often come from EMT, nursing, firefighting, military, or demolition backgrounds. The job requires sympathy without empathy, and some companies offer grief counselors. Workers last about eight months on average before burning out.

segments.title: Three main scene types: violent death, decomposition, meth labs
segments.summary: The hosts outline the three main scene types. Meth labs are highly toxic, with chemicals absorbed through skin and contaminating air, often requiring removal of drywall, floors and carpet down to the studs.

segments.title: Tools and equipment of the trade
segments.summary: Equipment includes protective suits, fifty-five gallon biowaste drums, hospital-strength disinfectants, ozone machines, foggers, enzyme solvents, shovels and bags for dried blood, putty knives and steamers for brain matter, no-touch cleaning systems, ladders, and cameras for insurance photos.
topics: before and after photos for insurance

segments.title: Decomposing bodies, maggots and odor
segments.summary: Decomposition causes swelling, insect infestation, and liquefaction. Cleaners must remove liquefied tissue and maggots, which are disposed of by burning. The ammonia-based odor is described as overpowering.

segments.title: Violent death scenes, costs and insurance
segments.summary: Shooting and suicide scenes involve the most blood and are the hardest. Cleanup can take a few hours to forty-eight hours. Companies charge several hundred dollars an hour, with a typical bloody room costing about one to three thousand dollars, and insurance or the Crime Victim Reparations agency may pay.

segments.title: Disposal, incineration and regulation
segments.summary: Biohazard waste cannot go in regular trash. It must be incinerated, often priced by the pound with minimum charges, and meth waste requires special permits and disposal sites. The industry is not nationally regulated but generally follows OSHA bloodborne pathogen standards.

segments.title: Training, gross-out tests, stress, and marketing
segments.summary: Companies test applicants' tolerance for gore, have them clean dead animal carcasses, and require hepatitis B vaccination. Workers face critical incident stress and secondary traumatic stress. Marketing relies on hotels, motels, detectives and ambulance drivers. The hosts debate whether profiting from tragedy is acceptable.

segments.title: Listener mail: prison life and slang
segments.summary: A former federal prison inmate writes about commissary food as currency, handball tournaments, two escapes from a camp, and prison slang such as shank, the shoe, keystering, and man walking. Hosts also reference an email about the title hyphenation.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh gives the email address for listener mail and points listeners to the HowStuffWorks website for more articles.
